keywords.technical_meaning: Returns rows when there is at least one match in both tables based on join condition.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT a.col1, b.col2 FROM TableA a INNER JOIN TableB b ON a.id = b.id
keywords.performance_notes: Ensure join columns are indexed with compatible data types to avoid implicit conversions.
common_pitfalls: Accidental Cartesian product if ON condition is omitted or incomplete.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns all rows from the left table, and matching rows from the right table, filling with NULL on mismatch.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT a.col1, b.col2 FROM TableA a LEFT JOIN TableB b ON a.id = b.id
keywords.performance_notes: Placing right-table predicates in WHERE clause effectively converts it into an INNER JOIN.
common_pitfalls: Filtering right table in WHERE clause instead of ON clause.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns all rows from the right table, and matching rows from the left table.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT a.col1, b.col2 FROM TableA a RIGHT JOIN TableB b ON a.id = b.id
keywords.performance_notes: Usually rewritten as LEFT JOIN for consistency and readability.
common_pitfalls: Confusion with table precedence.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns all rows when there is a match in one of the tables; unmatched rows contain NULL.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT a.col1, b.col2 FROM TableA a FULL OUTER JOIN TableB b ON a.id = b.id
keywords.performance_notes: Costly execution plan; requires scanning or hash matching both inputs completely.
common_pitfalls: High memory and CPU usage on large datasets.

keywords.technical_meaning: Produces the Cartesian product of rows from both tables.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT a.col1, b.col2 FROM TableA a CROSS JOIN TableB b
keywords.performance_notes: Results in N x M rows; can severely degrade performance on large tables.
common_pitfalls: Accidental Cartesian joins when WHERE or ON conditions are missing.

keywords.technical_meaning: Invokes a table-valued function or correlated subquery for each row of the outer table expression.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT c.id, recent.OrderDate FROM Customers c CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 OrderDate FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustId = c.id ORDER BY OrderDate DESC) recent
keywords.performance_notes: Similar to an inner join but evaluates the right side for each outer row.
common_pitfalls: Rows from outer table are omitted if right side returns empty set.

keywords.technical_meaning: Like CROSS APPLY but returns all outer rows, filling NULL if right side returns empty.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT c.id, recent.OrderDate FROM Customers c OUTER APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 OrderDate FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustId = c.id ORDER BY OrderDate DESC) recent
keywords.performance_notes: Preserves outer rows even if correlated subquery yields no records.
common_pitfalls: NULL handling on projected correlated columns.

keywords.technical_meaning: Filters rows before grouping or aggregation takes place.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Status = 1 AND Amount > 100
keywords.performance_notes: Sargable predicates enable index seek operations; avoid wrapping filtered columns in scalar functions.
common_pitfalls: Using scalar functions on index columns (e.g. YEAR(date) = 2023).
keywords.source_chapter: Chapter 22: Filter results using WHERE and HAVING

keywords.technical_meaning: Filters groups of rows after GROUP BY aggregation.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT DeptId, COUNT(*) FROM Employees GROUP BY DeptId HAVING COUNT(*) > 10
keywords.performance_notes: Cannot utilize indexes directly; filters after aggregation is computed.
common_pitfalls: Using HAVING for conditions that could be evaluated earlier in WHERE.
keywords.source_chapter: Chapter 22: Filter results using WHERE and HAVING

keywords.technical_meaning: Groups rows that have the same values in specified columns into summary rows.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Category, SUM(Sales) FROM Products GROUP BY Category
keywords.performance_notes: Requires sort or hash match aggregate in execution plan.
common_pitfalls: Selecting columns not included in GROUP BY or aggregate functions.

keywords.technical_meaning: Eliminates duplicate rows from query results.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT DISTINCT Country FROM Customers
keywords.performance_notes: Forces a sort or distinct hash match, which can be expensive.
common_pitfalls: Masking underlying join duplicates instead of fixing join conditions.
keywords.source_chapter: Chapter 49: SQL Group By vs Distinct

keywords.technical_meaning: Limits the number or percentage of rows returned by a query.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT TOP 10 * FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderDate DESC
keywords.performance_notes: Always pair with an ORDER BY for deterministic results.
common_pitfalls: Non-deterministic results if ORDER BY is omitted or ties exist without WITH TIES.

keywords.technical_meaning: Standard ANSI SQL paging mechanism skipping N rows and returning next M rows.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderDate DESC OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY
keywords.performance_notes: Requires an explicit ORDER BY clause.
common_pitfalls: High offset numbers scan and discard previous rows, increasing I/O.

keywords.technical_meaning: Sorts query results by one or more columns in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Customers ORDER BY LastName ASC, FirstName ASC
keywords.performance_notes: Can spill to tempdb if sort memory grant is exceeded.
common_pitfalls: Relying on physical row order without an explicit ORDER BY.

keywords.technical_meaning: Evaluates a list of conditions and returns one of multiple possible result expressions.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT CASE WHEN Status = 1 THEN 'Active' WHEN Status = 0 THEN 'Inactive' ELSE 'Unknown' END FROM T
keywords.performance_notes: Evaluated sequentially; order most frequent conditions first.
common_pitfalls: Omitting ELSE branch causes unmatched cases to return NULL.

keywords.technical_meaning: T-SQL specific function replacing NULL with specified replacement value.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT ISNULL(Phone, 'N/A') FROM Contacts
keywords.performance_notes: Returns datatype of first argument; faster than COALESCE for 2 parameters in T-SQL.
common_pitfalls: Truncates replacement value if its length exceeds datatype of first parameter.

keywords.technical_meaning: ANSI SQL standard function returning the first non-null expression among its arguments.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT COALESCE(Mobile, Home, Work, 'None') FROM Contacts
keywords.performance_notes: Determines data type based on highest data type precedence among all arguments.
common_pitfalls: Translates internally into a CASE expression, which may evaluate arguments multiple times.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns NULL if two expressions are equal; otherwise returns the first expression.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Total / NULLIF(Units, 0) FROM Sales
keywords.performance_notes: Commonly used to prevent divide-by-zero runtime errors.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting that NULLIF returns NULL on match.

keywords.technical_meaning: Shorthand function for writing CASE WHEN boolean_expression THEN true_value ELSE false_value END.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT IIF(Score >= 50, 'Pass', 'Fail') FROM ExamResults
keywords.performance_notes: Syntactic sugar over CASE; compiles to CASE in SQL Server.
common_pitfalls: T-SQL specific; not supported in older ANSI or certain other dialects.

keywords.technical_meaning: Converts an expression from one data type to another according to ANSI standard.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT CAST(Price AS INT) FROM Products
keywords.performance_notes: May cause non-sargable query plans if applied to indexed filter columns.
common_pitfalls: Raises query error if conversion is invalid; consider TRY_CAST.

keywords.technical_meaning: T-SQL conversion function supporting style formatting parameters for dates and binary data.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), GETDATE(), 120)
keywords.performance_notes: Style parameter 120 gives canonical ODBC standard YYYY-MM-DD HH:MI:SS.
common_pitfalls: Style codes vary across database versions; raises error on failure.

keywords.technical_meaning: Attempts type conversion and returns NULL if conversion fails, avoiding query errors.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT TRY_CAST(RawValue AS INT) FROM LegacyData
keywords.performance_notes: Safeguards ETL data cleansing against malformed string inputs.
common_pitfalls: Returns NULL for both legitimate NULLs and failed conversions.

keywords.technical_meaning: Extracts a portion of a string beginning at specified 1-based character position.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT SUBSTRING(PostalCode, 1, 3) FROM Addresses
keywords.performance_notes: Non-sargable when used on WHERE filter columns.
common_pitfalls: SQL Server string indices are 1-based, not 0-based.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns number of characters in string expression, excluding trailing blanks.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT LEN(ProductName) FROM Products
keywords.performance_notes: Ignores trailing spaces; use DATALENGTH to include trailing spaces and measure bytes.
common_pitfalls: DATALENGTH returns bytes (double for NVARCHAR), LEN returns characters.

keywords.technical_meaning: Converts lowercase characters in a string to uppercase.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT UPPER(LastName) FROM Customers
keywords.performance_notes: Can prevent index seek unless collation or computed column index is used.
common_pitfalls: Non-sargable predicate if used as UPPER(col) = 'VALUE'.

keywords.technical_meaning: Converts uppercase characters in a string to lowercase.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT LOWER(Email) FROM Users
keywords.performance_notes: Non-sargable predicate when applied to column expressions in WHERE.
common_pitfalls: May affect collation-sensitive comparisons.

keywords.technical_meaning: Removes leading spaces from string expression.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT LTRIM(Description) FROM Catalog
keywords.performance_notes: Used in data cleansing pipelines.
common_pitfalls: Only removes spaces, not tabs or other whitespace characters unless upgraded.

keywords.technical_meaning: Removes trailing spaces from string expression.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT RTRIM(LastName) FROM Customers
keywords.performance_notes: Used before concatenation to prevent extra gaps.
common_pitfalls: Only removes standard spaces.

keywords.technical_meaning: Searches for an expression in another expression and returns its starting 1-based position.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT CHARINDEX('@', Email) FROM Contacts
keywords.performance_notes: Returns 0 if sequence is not found.
common_pitfalls: Arguments order is (search_target, string_to_search).

keywords.technical_meaning: Deletes a specified length of characters and inserts new characters at specified start position.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT STUFF(Phone, 1, 3, '***') FROM Users
keywords.performance_notes: Commonly combined with FOR XML PATH for string aggregation in legacy T-SQL.
common_pitfalls: Negative or 0 start position returns NULL.

keywords.technical_meaning: Concatenates two or more strings, converting NULL arguments to empty strings implicitly.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT CONCAT(FirstName, ' ', LastName) FROM Employees
keywords.performance_notes: Safer than the + operator because it avoids NULL propagation.
common_pitfalls: Requires at least 2 arguments in SQL Server.

keywords.technical_meaning: In T-SQL string context, concatenates two string expressions. In numeric context, performs addition.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT FirstName + ' ' + LastName FROM Employees
keywords.performance_notes: If any operand is NULL, the entire concatenation result is NULL unless CONCAT_NULL_YIELDS_NULL is OFF.
common_pitfalls: NULL propagation trap: 'Hello ' + NULL yields NULL instead of 'Hello '.

keywords.technical_meaning: Pattern matching operator using % (any sequence) and _ (single character) wildcards.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Items WHERE Code LIKE 'MM_%'
keywords.performance_notes: Leading wildcards (e.g. '%term') prevent index seek and cause full table scans.
common_pitfalls: Escape character must be specified when searching for literal underscores or percent signs.

keywords.technical_meaning: Determines whether a specified value matches any value in a subquery or a list of literals.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Country IN ('US', 'CA', 'MX')
keywords.performance_notes: Internally converted to a series of OR conditions or semi-join.
common_pitfalls: Very large literal lists (thousands) should be placed into table variables or temp tables.

keywords.technical_meaning: Determines whether a value does not match any value in a list or subquery.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT CustId FROM BadAccounts WHERE CustId IS NOT NULL)
keywords.performance_notes: Dangerous with nullable columns: if subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN and returns zero rows.
common_pitfalls: NULL trap: returns 0 rows if set contains NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS.

keywords.technical_meaning: Tests for existence of any rows in a subquery, returning TRUE as soon as first row is found.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Payments p WHERE p.OrderId = o.Id)
keywords.performance_notes: Short-circuits execution; optimizer does not evaluate projected columns in subquery.
common_pitfalls: Writing SELECT * instead of SELECT 1 in EXISTS is fine but SELECT 1 is standard convention.

keywords.technical_meaning: Tests that no rows match the correlated subquery condition.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustId = c.Id)
keywords.performance_notes: Robust against NULL values, unlike NOT IN; preferred anti-semi-join construct.
common_pitfalls: Failure to correlate subquery leads to checking global existence instead of per-row.

keywords.technical_meaning: Combines results of two or more queries into single result set, removing duplicate rows.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT City FROM Suppliers UNION SELECT City FROM Customers
keywords.performance_notes: Requires sort or hash match to remove duplicates. Prefer UNION ALL if duplicates are acceptable.
common_pitfalls: Unnecessary performance overhead when rows are known to be distinct.

keywords.technical_meaning: Combines results of two or more queries including all duplicate rows without sorting.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT PartNo FROM WarehouseA UNION ALL SELECT PartNo FROM WarehouseB
keywords.performance_notes: Much faster than UNION as it performs no deduplication or sort operations.
common_pitfalls: Accidental duplicates in downstream reporting if inputs overlap.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns distinct rows from left query that are not output by right query.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT CustId FROM ActiveCustomers EXCEPT SELECT CustId FROM InactiveCustomers
keywords.performance_notes: Deduplicates left side before matching.
common_pitfalls: Order of queries matters; A EXCEPT B is not equal to B EXCEPT A.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns distinct rows that are output by both the left and right input queries.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT EmpId FROM TrainingA INTERSECT SELECT EmpId FROM TrainingB
keywords.performance_notes: Requires matching column count and compatible data types.
common_pitfalls: Omits non-matching rows and deduplicates matches.

keywords.technical_meaning: Specifies a temporary named result set (Common Table Expression) within execution scope of a statement.
keywords.tsql_example: WITH SalesSummary AS (SELECT RepId, SUM(Amt) AS Total FROM Sales GROUP BY RepId) SELECT * FROM SalesSummary WHERE Total > 1000
keywords.performance_notes: In SQL Server, CTEs are inline views and re-evaluated each time referenced unless materialized into temp table.
common_pitfalls: Referencing large non-materialized CTE multiple times re-executes query each time.

keywords.technical_meaning: A CTE that references itself, comprising an anchor member and a recursive member joined by UNION ALL.
keywords.tsql_example: WITH Hierarchy AS (SELECT Id, ManagerId, 0 AS Lvl FROM Emp WHERE ManagerId IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.Id, e.ManagerId, h.Lvl+1 FROM Emp e JOIN Hierarchy h ON e.ManagerId = h.Id) SELECT * FROM Hierarchy
keywords.performance_notes: Subject to MAXRECURSION limit (default 100 in SQL Server). Use OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) if needed.
common_pitfalls: Infinite loops if circular references exist in data without termination condition.

keywords.technical_meaning: Assigns sequential integer number to each row within partition of result set starting at 1.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Id, Category, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Category ORDER BY Sales DESC) AS rn FROM Items
keywords.performance_notes: Requires an explicit ORDER BY clause inside OVER (...).
common_pitfalls: Non-deterministic numbering if ORDER BY columns are not unique.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns rank of each row within partition, leaving gaps in rank values when ties occur.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Id, Score, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Score DESC) AS rnk FROM Exams
keywords.performance_notes: Leaves gaps for ties (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4).
common_pitfalls: Confusion with DENSE_RANK which produces consecutive rankings without gaps.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns rank of each row within partition without gaps in ranking values for ties.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Id, Score, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Score DESC) AS drnk FROM Exams
keywords.performance_notes: Produces continuous integer sequences (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 3).
common_pitfalls: Assuming ranks are unique across tie rows.

keywords.technical_meaning: Accesses data from a previous row in the same result set without using a self-join.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT OrderDate, Amount, LAG(Amount, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate) AS PrevAmt FROM Sales
keywords.performance_notes: Avoids costly self-joins when computing period-over-period differences.
common_pitfalls: Requires ORDER BY in OVER clause.

keywords.technical_meaning: Accesses data from a subsequent row in the same result set without using a self-join.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT OrderDate, Amount, LEAD(Amount, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate) AS NextAmt FROM Sales
keywords.performance_notes: Avoids self-joins for forward-looking differences.
common_pitfalls: Requires ORDER BY in OVER clause.

keywords.technical_meaning: Distributes rows in an ordered partition into a specified number of named groups.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT CustId, Spend, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY Spend DESC) AS Quartile FROM Customers
keywords.performance_notes: Partitions rows into roughly equal bucket counts.
common_pitfalls: Groups may not have identical counts if total rows are not evenly divisible.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns the sum of all values, or only DISTINCT values, in specified expression.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Category, SUM(Price) FROM Products GROUP BY Category
keywords.performance_notes: Ignores NULL values.
common_pitfalls: Arithmetic overflow error if sum exceeds data type limits (use BIGINT for large totals).

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns number of items found in group. COUNT(*) returns all rows; COUNT(col) ignores NULLs.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(col) FROM TableA
keywords.performance_notes: COUNT(*) is optimized by query engine to use the narrowest non-clustered index.
common_pitfalls: COUNT(column) does not count NULL rows, whereas COUNT(*) counts all rows.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns average of values in group, ignoring NULL values.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Category, AVG(CAST(Rating AS FLOAT)) FROM Reviews GROUP BY Category
keywords.performance_notes: Integer division trap: AVG of integer column returns integer truncated result.
common_pitfalls: Divide-by-zero if group is empty; integer truncation on integer columns.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns minimum value in expression.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT MIN(OrderDate) FROM Orders
keywords.performance_notes: Utilizes index seeks if column is leading column of an index.
common_pitfalls: Ignores NULLs.

keywords.technical_meaning: Returns maximum value in expression.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT MAX(OrderDate) FROM Orders
keywords.performance_notes: Fast Top/Bottom index seek if index exists.
common_pitfalls: Ignores NULLs.

keywords.technical_meaning: Temporary table stored in tempdb visible only to current user session.
keywords.tsql_example: CREATE TABLE #TempOrders (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Amt MONEY)
keywords.performance_notes: Can have indexes, statistics, and constraints, making them superior to large table variables.
common_pitfalls: Dropped automatically when session ends, but should be explicitly dropped when done.

keywords.technical_meaning: Global temporary table in tempdb visible to all sessions across SQL Server.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * INTO ##GlobalCache FROM MasterData
keywords.performance_notes: Shared across sessions; risk of concurrent name collisions.
common_pitfalls: Dropped when last session referencing it disconnects.

keywords.technical_meaning: Creates a new table and inserts resulting rows from query into it in a single operation.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * INTO #ActiveProducts FROM Products WHERE Discontinued = 0
keywords.performance_notes: Minimally logged under Bulk-Logged or Simple recovery model.
common_pitfalls: Fails if destination table already exists; copies columns without constraints or indexes.

keywords.technical_meaning: Performs insert, update, or delete operations on target table based on results of join with source.
keywords.tsql_example: MERGE TargetTable AS T USING SourceTable AS S ON T.id = S.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET T.v = S.v WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, v) VALUES (S.id, S.v);
keywords.performance_notes: Must be terminated with a semicolon in T-SQL.
common_pitfalls: Known concurrency bugs and race conditions in SQL Server under high concurrency.

keywords.technical_meaning: Table hint instructing query optimizer to read uncommitted rows (dirty reads).
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM LargeTable WITH (NOLOCK)
keywords.performance_notes: Avoids shared read locks; risks reading phantom, uncommitted, or duplicated data.
common_pitfalls: Dirty reads, missing records, or reading records twice due to allocation order scans.

keywords.technical_meaning: The logical sequence in which SQL query clauses are processed: FROM -> ON -> JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> WITH CUBE/ROLLUP -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> TOP/OFFSET.
keywords.tsql_example: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY
keywords.performance_notes: Explains why aliases created in SELECT cannot be used directly in WHERE.
common_pitfalls: Attempting to reference SELECT aliases in the WHERE clause.

keywords.technical_meaning: Removes one or more rows from a table or view based on optional WHERE condition.
keywords.tsql_example: DELETE FROM Orders WHERE Status = 'Cancelled'
keywords.performance_notes: Fully logged row-by-row operation; consider TRUNCATE for complete wipe.
common_pitfalls: Omitting WHERE clause deletes all records in table.

keywords.technical_meaning: Adds one or more rows to a table or view.
keywords.tsql_example: INSERT INTO Customers (Id, Name) VALUES (1, 'Acme')
keywords.performance_notes: Batched inserts and INSERT...SELECT are much faster than single row inserts.
common_pitfalls: Column list mismatch or identity insert restriction.

keywords.technical_meaning: Modifies table definition by adding, dropping, or altering columns and constraints.
keywords.tsql_example: ALTER TABLE Customers ADD Email VARCHAR(100) NULL
keywords.performance_notes: Adding NOT NULL columns requires default value or table rewrite.
common_pitfalls: Schema locks can block active transaction queues.

keywords.technical_meaning: Creates a new table in the database schema.
keywords.tsql_example: CREATE TABLE dbo.Items (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Code VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL)
keywords.performance_notes: Define explicit clustered primary keys on high-insert tables.
common_pitfalls: Missing primary keys or incorrect column collation.

keywords.technical_meaning: Creates a user-defined function returning a scalar value or a table result.
keywords.tsql_example: CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetTax (@amount MONEY) RETURNS MONEY AS BEGIN RETURN @amount * 0.1 END
keywords.performance_notes: Scalar UDFs in WHERE clauses prevent parallel execution and cause row-by-row RBAR overhead.
common_pitfalls: Calling scalar functions in query projection/filters severely hurts execution speed.

keywords.technical_meaning: A precompiled collection of one or more SQL statements and procedural control-of-flow logic.
keywords.tsql_example: CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.UpdateInventory @id INT, @qty INT AS BEGIN UPDATE Stock SET Qty = Qty - @qty WHERE Id = @id END
keywords.performance_notes: Execution plans are cached and reused; beware of parameter sniffing.
common_pitfalls: Parameter sniffing leading to suboptimal plan cache reuse.

keywords.technical_meaning: Creates a virtual table based on the result-set of an SQL statement.
keywords.tsql_example: CREATE VIEW dbo.ActiveUsers AS SELECT Id, Name FROM Users WHERE Active = 1
keywords.performance_notes: Unindexed views do not store data; inner query is expanded and executed at runtime.
common_pitfalls: Nesting views multiple levels deep creates severe query optimization bottlenecks.

keywords.technical_meaning: Modifies a previously created view without changing permissions or affecting dependent stored procedures.
keywords.tsql_example: ALTER VIEW dbo.ActiveUsers AS SELECT Id, Name, Role FROM Users WHERE Active = 1
keywords.performance_notes: Maintains view permissions while redefining the underlying query.
common_pitfalls: Column definitions and ordering may shift if SELECT * was used.

keywords.technical_meaning: Non-executable descriptive text embedded in SQL scripts; line comments (--) or block comments (/* */).
keywords.performance_notes: Stripped during parser normalization; untrusted in multi-agent environments.
common_pitfalls: Unclosed block comment /* comments out entire remaining script.

keywords.technical_meaning: Combines two boolean expressions and returns TRUE when both expressions evaluate to TRUE.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Status = 1 AND Amount > 100
keywords.performance_notes: Short-circuits in SQL Server query execution.
common_pitfalls: Operator precedence: AND binds more tightly than OR.

keywords.technical_meaning: Combines two boolean expressions and returns TRUE when either expression evaluates to TRUE.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Status = 1 OR Flag = 'X'
keywords.performance_notes: OR conditions on different columns frequently prevent index seeks and force index scans.
common_pitfalls: Mixing AND and OR without explicit parentheses causes logic bugs.

keywords.technical_meaning: A query nested inside a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement, or inside another subquery.
keywords.tsql_example: SELECT Name, (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Salaries WHERE EmpId = e.Id) FROM Employees e
keywords.performance_notes: Correlated subqueries execute once per outer row unless optimized into joins.
common_pitfalls: Subqueries in SELECT clause returning more than one scalar value will throw runtime errors.
